title: Come and See
subtitle: John in Poems & Pictures
author: Timothy Holt
beforeYouBegin:
John's gospel begins before the beginning and ends with breakfast on a beach. In between: water turned to wine, a woman at a well, bread for five thousand, a dead man called by name, a basin and a towel, a cross, and an empty tomb in a garden.

This book walks through it in forty short poems, in five parts. Each poem sits beside a picture and under a single line of Scripture. The pictures stay with the things around Jesus —jars, a well, a basin, a charcoal fire—and leave his face to your imagination.

The poems are not the Bible. They are one reader's response to it. Open the Gospel of John alongside this book, and let the real words have the last word.

parts.title: The Word Became Flesh
parts.epigraph: The W ord became flesh, and lived among us.
parts.lightName: Light of The Word Became Flesh

paintings.title: the W ord
paintings.epigraph: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.”
paintings.poem:
John starts where Genesis starts:
in the beginning.

but before the light,
before the land,
before anything was made—

the Word.

God has always
been speaking.
and the sentence
has a name.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “the W ord” (John 1:1–3)—where the poem notes, “and the sentence has a name”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: not overcome
paintings.epigraph: “The light shines in the darkness, and the darkness hasn’t overcome it.”
paintings.poem:
the darkness
has had every chance.

wars. plagues.
empires. graves.
your worst year.

and the light
is still shining.

not because the dark is weak.
because the light
is him.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “not overcome” (John 1:4–5)—where the poem notes, “because the light is him”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: among us
paintings.epigraph: “full of grace and truth.”
paintings.poem:
the Word became flesh—
skin, hunger, calluses,
a hometown,
a trade.

he pitched his tent
among us,
the old word says,
like God in the desert—

but closer.
close enough
to touch.

grace
and truth,
walking around
in sandals.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “among us” (John 1:14)—where the poem notes, “walking around in sandals”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: the Lamb
paintings.epigraph: “Behold, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world!”
paintings.poem:
John the Baptist
saw his cousin walking up the riverbank
and said the strangest thing:

look—
the Lamb.

every lamb on every altar,
every doorframe in Egypt,
every Passover—

they were all
pointing
at him.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “the Lamb” (John 1:29)—where the poem notes, “pointing at him”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: come and see
paintings.epigraph: “Come, and see.”
paintings.poem:
they asked him
where he was staying.

he didn't give them an address
or a sermon.

come and see.

and they spent the day with him,
and one of them
remembered the time:
about four in the afternoon.

that's what meeting Jesus does.
you remember the hour.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “come and see” (John 1:35–39)—where the poem notes, “that's what meeting Jesus does. you remember the hour”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: the good wine
paintings.epigraph: “You have kept the good wine until now!”
paintings.poem:
the first sign
wasn't a healing.
it was a party
that ran out of wine.

six stone jars of water,
and the best wine
anyone had ever tasted.

he cares about
the embarrassed host,
the empty cups,
your joy.

and he saves
the best
for last.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “the good wine” (John 2:1–10)—where the poem notes, “the best for last”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: the wind
paintings.epigraph: “The wind blows where it wants to”
paintings.poem:
Nicodemus came at night,
a teacher with questions.

and Jesus pointed
at the wind.

you hear it.
you can't see it.
you can't steer it.

that's how new birth works:
not a program.
a breath from God
blowing where it wants—

sometimes
right through a teacher
at night.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “the wind” (John 3:1–8)—where the poem notes, “right through a teacher at night”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: so
paintings.epigraph: “For God so loved the world, that he gave his one and only Son”
paintings.poem:
the most famous verse
in the Bible
turns on a small word:
so.

so much.
so far.
so completely.

God loved the world
so
that he gave.

not a little.
not his leftovers.
his Son.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “so” (John 3:16)—where the poem notes, “not his leftovers. his Son”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: the jar left behind
paintings.epigraph: “the water that I will give him will become in him a well of water springing up to eternal life.”
paintings.poem:
she came at noon,
when no one else would be there.

and a Jewish man
asked her for a drink.

he offered her water
you never have to come back for—
a spring
inside you.

she left her jar
at the well.

when you find the spring,
you stop carrying
the bucket.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “the jar left behind” (John 4:13–15)—where the poem notes, “you stop carrying the bucket”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: everything I ever did
paintings.epigraph: “Come, see a man who told me everything that I did.”
paintings.poem:
he told me everything I ever did,
she said—

and she ran to tell the town.

not ashamed.
free.

the one who knew everything about her
had not turned away.

that's the kind of news
you run with.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “everything I ever did” (John 4:28–30)—where the poem notes, “that's the kind of news you run with”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: do you want to be well?
paintings.epigraph: “Do you want to be made well?”
paintings.poem:
thirty-eight years by the pool.

and Jesus asked
what sounds like a strange question:
do you want to be well?

because sometimes
we've been lying by the water
so long
we've made a home of the waiting.

get up, he said.
pick up your mat.
walk.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Where does your soul feel dry today, and how can you sink your roots deeper into the living water of John 5:5–9?

paintings.title: five and two
paintings.epigraph: “There is a boy here who has five barley loaves and two fish, but what are these among so many?”
paintings.poem:
five thousand people,
and one boy's lunch.

what is this
among so many?

a fair question.
the math doesn't work.

but the boy gave it anyway,
and Jesus gave thanks,

and there was enough.

bring what you have.
it was never the math
that fed them.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “five and two” (John 6:8–11)—where the poem notes, “it was never the math that fed them”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: nothing lost
paintings.epigraph: “Gather up the broken pieces which are left over, that nothing be lost.”
paintings.poem:
everyone had eaten.
there was plenty.

and still he said:
gather the broken pieces.
don't let anything be lost.

twelve baskets
of leftovers.

he's like that
with broken pieces—
of bread,
and of people.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “nothing lost” (John 6:12–13)—where the poem notes, “of bread, and of people”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: it is I
paintings.epigraph: “It is I. Don’t be afraid.”
paintings.poem:
dark.
wind.
miles from shore.

and someone walking toward them
on the water.

they were terrified.

and then the voice they knew:
it is I.
don't be afraid.

the thing coming toward you
in the storm
might be
him.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: What anxious weight can you place into the hands of the One who says, “Be still” and walks beside you in John 6:16–21?

paintings.title: where else?
paintings.epigraph: “Lord, to whom would we go? You have the words of eternal life.”
paintings.poem:
the crowds left.
the teaching was too hard.

and Jesus turned to the twelve:
do you want to leave too?

and Peter said
the most honest thing a doubter can say:

where else would we go?

you have
the words of life.

sometimes faith
is just knowing
there's nowhere else.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “where else?” (John 6:66–69)—where the poem notes, “is just knowing there's nowhere else”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: the light of the world
paintings.epigraph: “I am the light of the world.”
paintings.poem:
at the feast,
the temple courts
blazed with light.

and Jesus stood there
and said:
I am the light of the world.

not a light.
the light.

follow me,
and you won't walk
in the dark.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: What single step right in front of you is already lit by His word today, even if the far horizon remains unseen (John 8:12)?

paintings.title: the key
paintings.epigraph: “You will know the truth, and the truth will make you free.”
paintings.poem:
not an idea
that sets you free.

a person.

stay with my word, he said,
and you'll know the truth—

and the truth
isn't a lock.
it's a key.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “the key” (John 8:31–32)—where the poem notes, “isn't a lock. it's a key”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: one thing I know
paintings.epigraph: “though I was blind, now I see.”
paintings.poem:
the experts argued.
the parents hedged.
the neighbors weren't sure.

and the man born blind
said:
I don't know about all that.

one thing I know.
I was blind.
now I see.

you don't need to win the argument
to tell
what he did.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “one thing I know” (John 9:24–25)—where the poem notes, “to tell what he did”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: by name
paintings.epigraph: “He calls his own sheep by name, and leads them out.”
paintings.poem:
not a number.
not a flock.

by name.

the shepherd
knows the one who limps,
the one who wanders,
the one who's always last.

and the sheep
know his voice
from every other.

listen.
he's calling
yours.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: In the quiet after the noise, what gentle truth from John 10:2–4 (“he's calling yours”) is asking for your unhurried attention today?

paintings.title: the gate
paintings.epigraph: “The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep.”
paintings.poem:
a hired hand
runs when the wolf comes.

it's not his flock.

the good shepherd
lies down in the gateway
and says:
you'll have to go through me.

and the sheep
go free.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you pause at the threshold of “the gate” (John 10:11–15), what closed place in your life is waiting for you to open to His presence?

paintings.title: Jesus wept
paintings.epigraph: “Jesus wept.”
paintings.poem:
the shortest verse.

he knew
what he was about to do.
in a few minutes
Lazarus would walk out.

and still
he wept.

God doesn't skip your grief
on the way to the miracle.

he stands at the grave
and cries
with you.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “Jesus wept” (John 11:32–36)—where the poem notes, “and cries with you”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: unbind him
paintings.epigraph: “Free him, and let him go.”
paintings.poem:
Lazarus, come out!

and the dead man walked,
still wrapped in grave clothes.

and Jesus turned to the crowd:
unbind him.
let him go.

he gives the life.
he lets us
help with the wrappings.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “unbind him” (John 11:43–44)—where the poem notes, “he lets us help with the wrappings”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: the fragrance
paintings.epigraph: “The house was filled with the fragrance of the ointment.”
paintings.poem:
a year's wages,
poured on his feet.

Judas called it waste.

but the whole house
filled with the smell of it.

love that costs something
can't be kept quiet.
it fills the room.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “the fragrance” (John 12:1–5)—where the poem notes, “can't be kept quiet. it fills the room”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: the grain
paintings.epigraph: “unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains by itself alone”
paintings.poem:
a seed kept safe in a jar
stays a seed.

bury it,
and it becomes a field.

he was talking
about himself.

and he was talking
about us.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “the grain” (John 12:24)—where the poem notes, “and he was talking about us”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: twelve pairs
paintings.epigraph: “he poured water into the basin, and began to wash the disciples’ feet”
paintings.poem:
knowing he had all authority,
knowing where he came from,
knowing where he was going—

he got up from supper,
wrapped a towel around his waist,
and knelt.

twelve pairs of dirty feet,
including the ones
that would walk out
to betray him.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “twelve pairs” (John 13:3–5)—where the poem notes, “that would walk out to betray him”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: it was night
paintings.epigraph: “he went out immediately. It was night.”
paintings.poem:
Judas took the bread
and went out.

and John writes
four words:
it was night.

and not only
in the sky.

the saddest thing
isn't the dark.
it's leaving the table
where the light is.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “it was night” (John 13:26–30)—where the poem notes, “it's leaving the table where the light is”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: many rooms
paintings.epigraph: “In my Father’s house are many homes.”
paintings.poem:
don't let your hearts be troubled.

there's room
in my Father's house.
lots of rooms.

I'm going ahead
to get yours ready.

if it weren't true,
I would have told you.

he's not the kind
to leave you
guessing.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “many rooms” (John 14:1–3)—where the poem notes, “to leave you guessing”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: the way
paintings.epigraph: “I am the way, the truth, and the life.”
paintings.poem:
Thomas said:
we don't know where you're going.
how can we know the way?

and Jesus didn't hand him a map.

I am the way.

not directions.
a person
to walk with.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “the way” (John 14:5–6)—where the poem notes, “a person to walk with”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: peace
paintings.epigraph: “Peace I leave with you. My peace I give to you”
paintings.poem:
the night before the cross,
he gave them
what he had:

peace.

not the world's kind,
the absence of trouble.

his kind:
a calm heart
in the middle of it.

don't be troubled.
don't be afraid.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: What anxious weight can you place into the hands of the One who says, “Be still” and walks beside you in John 14:27?

paintings.title: the vine
paintings.epigraph: “I am the vine. Y ou are the branches.”
paintings.poem:
a branch
doesn't try hard
to make grapes.

it just stays
connected.

remain in me, he said,
and the fruit will come.

apart from me,
nothing.

with me,
more than you'd imagine.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “the vine” (John 15:4–5)—where the poem notes, “with me, more than you'd imagine”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: friends
paintings.epigraph: “I have called you friends”
paintings.poem:
not servants.
friends.

a servant does what he's told
without knowing why.

a friend
gets told everything.

and the greatest love,
he said,
is laying down your life
for your friends.

he was about to
show them.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “friends” (John 15:13–15)—where the poem notes, “he was about to show them”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: take heart
paintings.epigraph: “In the world you have trouble; but cheer up! I have overcome the world.”
paintings.poem:
he didn't promise
no trouble.

in the world
you will have trouble.
guaranteed.

but—
take heart.

I have overcome the world.

past tense,
the night before the cross.

he was that sure.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “take heart” (John 16:33)—where the poem notes, “he was that sure”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: what is truth?
paintings.epigraph: “What is truth?”
paintings.poem:
Pilate asked
the right question,

to the right person,

and walked out
before the answer.

truth was standing
right in front of him,
with bound hands.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “what is truth?” (John 18:37–38)—where the poem notes, “right in front of him, with bound hands”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: a family
paintings.epigraph: “From that hour, the disciple took her to his own home.”
paintings.poem:
dying,
he was still taking care of people.

his mother
needed a son.
his friend
needed a mother.

here's your son.
here's your mother.

and from that hour
the church began
as a family.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “a family” (John 19:25–27)—where the poem notes, “the church began as a family”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: finished
paintings.epigraph: “It is finished.”
paintings.poem:
one word:
paid in full.
done.
complete.

not "I am finished. "
it is finished.

everything he came to do.
everything the lambs pointed to.
everything we couldn't.

done.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “finished” (John 19:28–30)—where the poem notes, “done”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: while it was still dark
paintings.epigraph: “Mary Magdalene went early, while it was still dark, to the tomb”
paintings.poem:
she went while it was still dark—

not expecting anything.
just to be near him.

and the stone
was already gone.

sometimes the dawn
comes while it's still dark,
and we're the last
to find out.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Where is God inviting you to set down your work today and rest in what He has already finished (John 20:1)?

paintings.title: Mary
paintings.epigraph: “Jesus said to her, “Mary.””
paintings.poem:
she thought he was the gardener.

she was crying,
asking where they'd taken him.

and he said
one word:

Mary.

and she knew.

that's how he finds us—
not with an argument.
with our name.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “Mary” (John 20:11–16)—where the poem notes, “not with an argument. with our name”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: you
paintings.epigraph: “Blessed are those who have not seen, and have believed.”
paintings.poem:
Thomas wanted proof.
he got it—
the scars, the hands.

and Jesus looked past him,
two thousand years ahead,

and blessed you.

you haven't seen.
you believe anyway.

he says
you're blessed.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “you” (John 20:26–29)—where the poem notes, “he says you're blessed”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: breakfast
paintings.epigraph: “Come and eat breakfast!”
paintings.poem:
they'd fished all night
and caught nothing.

and on the shore,
a fire already going,
fish on the coals,
bread,

and the risen Lord
saying:
come have breakfast.

he could have said anything.
he said,
you must be hungry.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “breakfast” (John 21:9–12)—where the poem notes, “he said, you must be hungry”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: feed my sheep
paintings.epigraph: “Lord, you know everything. Y ou know that I have affection for you.”
paintings.poem:
a charcoal fire—
the same kind
Peter stood beside
when he denied him three times.

and now, by another fire,
three questions:
do you love me?

three times,
one for each denial.

and every time,
not a rebuke.
a job:

feed my sheep.

that's how he restores us.
he gives us
something to do.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “feed my sheep” (John 21:15–17)—where the poem notes, “he gives us something to do”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?
